name: Denileukin diftitox

lead:
Denileukin diftitox is a fusion protein that joins interleukin-2 to a diphtheria-toxin fragment so that it kills cells carrying the IL-2 receptor. It is approved for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, a skin-involving cancer.
Its place in hair discussions comes from alopecia areata, an autoimmune hair-loss condition in which T cells attack follicles. The idea is that removing activated T cells could allow hair to regrow, which would restore hair and the look of the scalp, brows and beard. Denileukin diftitox is used for lymphoma; no published alopecia areata trial exists.

paras: It is given by intravenous infusion in a clinic as a cancer therapy, in cycles under specialist supervision. It is not a cosmetic or self-administered product.

The US label carries a boxed warning for capillary leak syndrome. Other reported effects include infusion reactions, liver-enzyme elevation, low albumin, edema, fatigue, rash and visual impairment.[1]

angle.text: Alopecia areata involves T-cell attack on follicles, and denileukin diftitox removes IL-2 receptor-bearing T cells. Interest in it for hair rests on that mechanism rather than on hair-loss trial results.

lead: Denileukin diftitox is an antineoplastic immunotoxin: interleukin-2 fused to diphtheria-toxin fragments, which binds IL-2 receptors and halts protein synthesis in the cell.[1] Ontak received US accelerated approval for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL) in 1999, was withdrawn in 2014 amid supply problems, and a reformulated version, Lymphir (denileukin diftitox-cxdl), was approved in 2024.[1]

For appearance, the interest is indirect. Alopecia areata involves T-cell attack on hair follicles, so drugs that deplete activated T cells are of theoretical interest for regrowing scalp, brow and beard hair. The published denileukin diftitox literature gathered here concerns lymphoma and other cancers; no human alopecia areata trial appears in it.
A phase III registrational trial of denileukin diftitox-cxdl in relapsed or refractory CTCL reported an objective response rate of 36.2 percent among 69 patients in the primary analysis.[2]

paras: In the US, Lymphir is indicated for adults with relapsed or refractory stage I-III CTCL after at least one systemic therapy.[1] Reviews describe earlier use of Ontak in CTCL and examined other tumour settings.[3][4]

The IL-2 portion binds IL-2 receptors; the complex is internalised and the toxin stops protein synthesis.[1] It also transiently reduces regulatory T cells, a property explored with cancer vaccines.[5]

Common effects include liver-enzyme elevation, low albumin, nausea, edema, fatigue, rash and chills; serious ones include capillary leak syndrome (boxed warning), infusion reactions, hepatotoxicity and visual impairment.[1]
Accelerated approval 1999; full approval 2008; US withdrawal 2014; reformulated E7777 approved in Japan in 2021 and in the US in August 2024.[1]

Human studies cover CTCL, including a phase III trial of the improved-purity formulation, a phase III analysis of placebo-arm remissions in CD25-positive disease, a phase II study in CD25-low disease, and exploratory trials in lung and ovarian cancer.[2][6][7][8][9] No clinical studies in alopecia areata or other hair loss were found.
